common.noShift: No shift: no motion along our line of sight

doppler.waveNote: Not to scale: the star's speed is hugely exaggerated compared with the speed of light.
doppler.explanationTitle: Measuring a star's speed with light
doppler.explanation1: Atoms in a star's outer layers absorb light at exact wavelengths, so its spectrum is crossed by dark lines. We know where these lines belong from measurements in the laboratory.
doppler.explanation2: If the star moves away from us, each light wave is stretched: the lines move to longer, redder wavelengths (a redshift). If it moves toward us, the waves are squeezed and the lines move to shorter, bluer wavelengths (a blueshift).
doppler.explanation3: Only motion along our line of sight shifts the lines. Comparing each line with its lab position gives that speed, the radial velocity: Δλ / λ = v<sub>r</sub> / c.
doppler.explanation4: The shifts are tiny. A star wobbling at 10 m/s moves a line by about 0.00002 nm, so astronomers need very stable spectrographs that compare thousands of lines at once.

wobble.telescopeCaption: This is all an astronomer gets: the planet is far too faint to see next to its star. We detect the planet only through the star's light.
wobble.explanationTitle: A planet makes its star wobble
wobble.explanation1: A star and its planet both orbit their common center of mass. The star is much heavier, so the center of mass sits very close to the star (often inside it), and the star moves in a tiny circle.
wobble.explanation2: As the star circles, it moves toward us for half the orbit and away for the other half. Its spectral lines shift blue, then red, then blue again, once per orbit.
wobble.explanation3: We never see the planet. We measure the star's radial velocity night after night: the repeating pattern reveals the planet. The time for one cycle is the planet's orbital period, and the size of the swing tells us its mass.
wobble.explanation4: Heavier planets and closer planets give bigger, faster wobbles, which is why the first planets found this way were giant planets very close to their stars ("hot Jupiters").

viewingAngle.chartTitle: Star's radial velocity over one orbit
viewingAngle.faceOnWarning: Face-on: the star moves only across the sky, never toward or away from us. No Doppler shift: the planet goes undetected!
viewingAngle.equation: K = v<sub>★</sub> sin i       M<sub>p</sub> sin i ≤ M<sub>p</sub>
viewingAngle.explanation1: The Doppler effect only measures the part of the star's motion along our line of sight. How much of the wobble we see depends on how the orbit is tilted toward Earth.
viewingAngle.explanation2: Seen edge-on (tilt 90°), the star moves straight toward and away from us: we see the full wobble. Seen face-on (tilt 0°), the star moves only across the sky: no shift at all, and the planet is invisible to this method.
viewingAngle.explanation3: In between, we measure the full speed multiplied by sin i. Since we usually don't know the tilt, we can only find a minimum mass, M<sub>p</sub> sin i: the true planet may be heavier.
viewingAngle.explanation4: Changing Earth's direction within the orbital plane does not change the size of the signal, only when in the orbit the star is moving toward us.

observatory.noPlanetAnswer: Answer: this star's wobble is far below the noise.
observatory.explanationTitle: Finding a planet in the data
observatory.explanation1: Each night you can observe, the spectrograph gives one radial velocity, with some measurement error (the error bar).
observatory.explanation2: Collect measurements over several orbits, then adjust your model: the period sets how often the pattern repeats, the amplitude sets its size, and the phase slides it in time.
observatory.explanation3: When your model is good, folding the data on your period stacks all the orbits into one clean curve, and the scatter about your model drops to about the measurement error.
observatory.explanation4: From the period, the amplitude and the star's mass you get the planet's minimum mass. Try Sun + Earth: its 9 cm/s wobble is far below ±1 m/s, which is why Earth twins are so hard to find.
